clinicalPearls: Atelosteogenesis is a group of severe short-limbed skeletal dysplasias whose name literally means incomplete ossification of bone.

Three types are recognised: types I and III are caused by dominant, usually de novo, variants in FLNB (filamin B), whereas type II is autosomal recessive due to SLC26A2 (the diastrophic dysplasia sulfate transporter, DTDST).
Types I and II are typically lethal in the perinatal period; type III is the mildest and some affected individuals survive infancy with variable disability.
Characteristic radiographic features include rhizomelic limb shortening, hypoplastic or absent distal humeri and femora, dislocated large joints, clubfeet and coronal or sagittal vertebral clefts.
Type II shares features with diastrophic dysplasia and achondrogenesis type IB (all SLC26A2 sulfation-pathway disorders), including cleft palate and abducted hitchhiker thumbs.
The FLNB-related types belong to a filaminopathy spectrum that also includes Larsen syndrome and boomerang dysplasia.
A distinctive facies with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia is common, and a small thorax drives respiratory insufficiency in the lethal forms.
Antenatal ultrasound may detect severe micromelia and joint dislocations; molecular testing is needed to distinguish the subtypes and their differing recurrence risks.
reference.pathophysiology: Atelosteogenesis is genetically heterogeneous. Types I and III arise from dominant, usually de novo, gain-of-function or dominant-negative variants in FLNB, which encodes filamin B, an actin-crosslinking cytoskeletal protein essential for chondrocyte differentiation, vertebral segmentation and joint formation; these belong to the FLNB filaminopathy spectrum. Type II is autosomal recessive and results from biallelic variants in SLC26A2, a sulfate/chloride antiporter that supplies inorganic sulfate for proteoglycan sulfation in cartilage; deficient activity yields undersulfated cartilage matrix, placing it within the recessive sulfation-defect chondrodysplasia family alongside diastrophic dysplasia and achondrogenesis type IB. Failure of normal endochondral ossification produces the hypoplastic and dislocated appendicular skeleton, vertebral clefts and small thorax that define the group.
additionalDifferentials: Boomerang dysplasia (FLNB, allelic with atelosteogenesis type I)
additionalInvestigations: Chondro-osseous histology, including giant-cell chondrocytes in type I
Cartilage sulfation studies or fibroblast sulfate uptake for the recessive form
Perinatal pathology examination with clinical photography
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory insufficiency arising from a small, narrow thorax
Severe micromelia with multiple joint dislocations on antenatal scanning
A lethal course requiring perinatal palliative planning and family support
Airway compromise from laryngeal or tracheal cartilage involvement
reference.prognosis: Types I and II are usually lethal in the perinatal period, most often from pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory failure. Type III is milder, with survival and variable orthopaedic, spinal and respiratory morbidity.
pitfalls: Conflating the three types, which differ in gene, inheritance and recurrence risk
Assuming all cases are lethal when type III survivors exist
Overlooking that dominant FLNB disease is usually de novo with low recurrence, whereas recessive SLC26A2 disease carries higher recurrence
Misclassifying type II as diastrophic dysplasia given their clinical overlap
management: Prenatal diagnosis and counselling, with a palliative and comfort-care pathway offered for the perinatally lethal types I and II
Neonatal respiratory support for pulmonary hypoplasia and airway compromise, with intensive-care decisions guided by prognosis
Airway assessment and management of cleft palate and cervical-spine instability, particularly in the SLC26A2-related type II
Orthopaedic management of joint dislocations, clubfeet and spinal deformity in survivors of the milder type III
Multidisciplinary follow-up across clinical genetics, orthopaedics, respiratory medicine and spinal surgery for surviving children

Genetic counselling: recurrence risk is typically low for the de novo dominant FLNB types (I and III) but follows autosomal recessive inheritance for the SLC26A2 type II, with prenatal testing offered
